title: Continue reading in APP
body:
Before my pay hit the pack account, Mom's text lit up my screen. 
[Deposit day, sweetie! Don't forget - the pack tithe this month.] 
I stared at it. Then typed back. 
[My fang's infected. Can I keep an extra three hundred to get it looked at?] 
She immediately phoned and howled. 
"Healers don't charge that much." 
"Lance's Alpha trials are coming up. Every coin counts." 
"Keep fifty. Buy some painleaf." 
I hung up and opened the pack feed, scrolling for a cheap healer. 
That's when a photo stopped me cold. 
Roasted elk haunch. Silverbrook wine. Truffle-stuffed pheasant. 
[Lance dominated the Moon Run today! Only the best for my future Alpha ⚽] 
My jaw throbbed. 
The swelling pressed against my cheek, heat radiating up to my temple. 
Then I opened my contacts and mind-linked the wolf two thousand miles away. 
[I'll take the territory post. When can I start?]

Mom's pack feed account, "The Perfect Pack," had posted again thirty minutes ago.

In the photo, my brother Lance held up a rack of ribs bigger than his forearm, grinning like he'd already won Alpha of the Year.

Dad carved the meat for him. Mom held the phone, her face glowing with pure worship.

I locked my screen.

The throbbing pain from my infected fang shot straight through my skull.

This was my pack - the wolves who treated me like a tithe collector and Lance like a moon-blessed prince.

The only wolf who actually cared about me was Grandmother, and she lived three territories away.

I opened my contacts and found the one labeled "Southern Range - Pack Relations."

[Hi, is that position in the Houston territory still open?]

The reply came instantly.

[Allie? Our Alpha was deeply impressed by you. You can start whenever you're ready.]

[Thank you. I can arrive by the next full moon to handle the blood oath.]

I opened my tablet and drafted my den-abandonment notice, then sent it to my pack superior.

Three hours later, I sat in a back-alley healer den at the edge of a strip mall.

No numbing herbs - that would've been extra.

I checked my pack account balance: eight hundred and forty-seven credits. I shook my head. "Healer, just pull it. I can handle the pain."

The silver-plated pliers clamped down. I heard the sickening crunch of my fang being pried loose.

Pain exploded through my jaw.

My whole body went rigid. A growl clawed at my throat, but I swallowed it.

Sweat rolled down my temples and into my eyes, stinging and bitter.

When the fang finally tore free, the world went black for a heartbeat. Everything spun.

One thought screamed in my head: Hold it together. This is the first step to leaving them. This is what freedom costs.

The healer dropped the bloody fang onto a tray and gave me a grim smile.

"Girl, you've got guts. Most wolves would've shifted from the pain."

"Thanks."

Life forced me to.

I rinsed my mouth, spat pink into the basin, and left.

The second I got back to my shoebox den with its flimsy partition wall, Mom's howl filled my mind-link, then my phone, then both at once.

I answered. Before I could say a word, she exploded.

"Allie! What in the Moon's name do you think you're doing? You can't just abandon your pack post!"

My superior must've told her. He was Mom's second cousin - the wolf who got me that posting as a "favor" she never let me forget.

"I'm done with it. That's all."

"Done with it? Are you feral? What about next month's tithe? Are we supposed to starve? Lance is entering Alpha Academy next season - his sponsorship fee is due! How are we supposed to cover that without you?"

I listened to her screeching and felt something snap inside my ch//est. Deep. Final.

"Mother, I earn three thousand credits a month. Not thirty thousand."

"So what? Three thousand is still tribute!"

"You lived in our den for years. Now that you're earning, helping with Lance's Alpha path is the least you can do. You know how expensive cross-territory academies are!"

"And don't forget - I'm the wolf who got you that posting in the first place. You trying to bare your fangs at me now?"

I'd moved out of the pack den right after my coming-of-age run. But I'd still been sending nearly my full tithe home every month.

Not because I lived there. I didn't.

Because Mother said it was my "duty as a daughter of the pack."

When I didn't respond, she kept going.

"You ungrateful mutt! I should've never whelped you! Think you're too good for us now? Let me tell you something. You're not going anywhere. You're bound to us. You'll be serving me, your father, and Lance for the rest of your moons!"

I stayed silent until she ran out of breath.

"Mother, are you finished? Because I'm ending the link now."

Before she could reply, I severed the connection and blocked her from every channel.

My den fell silent.

I stood in the middle of that tiny room, my jaw still throbbing, blood still faintly metallic on my tongue.

And for the first time in twenty-five years, I could hear myself breathe.

The next morning, I went to the pack administration den to finalize my severance.

My superior - Mom's second cousin, the one who'd held this over my head for years - leaned back in his chair and gave me a long, patronizing stare.

"Allie, I'm not trying to be harsh. But your mother howled through the mind-link in tears. She's devastated."

"Look. Maybe they pamper Lance a bit much. But she's still your dam. Pack is pack. A she-wolf's best path is staying close to the den, tending to her elders, helping her litter-mate rise."

"When you find a mate, he can contribute to the family tithe too. Everyone wins."

"We're all just regular wolves trying to get by. Three thousand credits a month isn't bad. Why make things harder on yourself? You leave now, you're starting from scratch with no pack protection. Not worth it."

I stared at him. Kept my silence.

"Listen to me. Run home, bare your throat to your mother, and I'll pretend I never got this den-abandonment notice. Deal?"

I slid the separation parchment across his desk.

"Sign it."

His expression darkened instantly. His scent soured with anger. "You're really going to throw this back in my face?"

He signed.

I didn't say another word. I walked straight to the pack records keeper.

He followed me into the corridor, fangs half-bared. "Allie! You're going to regret this! A lone wolf doesn't last!"

I didn't look back.

The only thing I regretted was not leaving sooner.

The exit rites were surprisingly smooth.

Probably because nobody thought a wolf earning three thousand credits a month was worth fighting for.

I left the administration den and started erasing every trace of my life in this territory.

The den was a rental. Easy to walk away from.

All the furniture and clutter I couldn't take with me, I listed on the territory trading board for a single silver coin.

A young she-wolf, fresh from her coming-of-age run, contacted me.

When she saw everything, her eyes went wide. "Are you serious? All of this for one silver?"

"Yes. But you have to take it all today."

She summoned her friends and a hauling service within the hour.

By late afternoon, my tiny den was empty except for one leather travel pack and my satchel.

I stood in the hollow space. Dust motes floated in the dying light.

I breathed in. Breathed out.

Felt lighter than I had in years.

Then my phone buzzed.

A message from Lance.

[What's your damage? You seriously blocked our mother? She nearly went feral. Unblock her. Now.]

Then one from Father.

[You ungrateful whelp. You blocked your own dam? You think I won't track your scent to that office and drag you back by your tail?]

Lance always sided with Mother. Always.

Father barely acknowledged my existence unless Mother ordered him to apply pressure.

Now? I blocked them both. And every unknown number. And every mind-link probe that tried to reach me after that.

My phone went silent.

My mind went silent.

I booked passage on a moon-runner heading south at dawn.

That night, I stayed in a cheap wayfarer's lodge near the territory edge.

My jaw still ached from the fang extraction. A dull, deep throb that pulsed with every heartbeat.

But I slept better than I had in years.

It was the most peaceful rest I'd had since my coming-of-age. No pack duties. No howling demands. No guilt seeping through the mind-link.

Just silence.

At first light, I dragged my pack to the departure point.

Just as I was about to cross the gate, Father appeared.

Out of breath. Eyes wild. Blocking my path.

"Allie! Where in the Moon's name do you think you're going? You're really leaving the territory?"

I looked at him.

Felt absolutely nothing.

"Father, move."

He grabbed my travel pack. His claws dimpled the leather. "You can't do this! What about the pack? What about your brother's future?"

I was so tired of this.

"Let go."

He dropped onto my pack like a pup throwing a tantrum, right there on the dirt path. Travelers stared. Wolves from other packs averted their eyes.

"I'm not moving unless you swear a blood oath to stay! If you walk away from your own blood, I'll - I'll go feral right here!"

The departure gate was packed. Wolves and humans alike kept glancing our way.

"Everyone, witness this!" Father bellowed, slapping his thigh like a street performer. "My own daughter! She's abandoning her pack just so she can run off and play lone wolf!"

He was practically howling now, really selling it.

I watched him perform and almost laughed. This was my father - the wolf who only showed up when he needed tribute money.

"Father, are you done? This is a public den."

"Allie! You're the one forcing my claws! Your mother's in the healer's ward because of YOU, and you're still trying to run? Do you even have a wolf's heart?!"

I paused.

Then I understood. Another one of their manipulations.

"Really? Which healer's ward? I'll go see her right now."

His eyes shifted. His scent flickered with panic. "Never mind which ward! Just come back to the den with me!"

I pulled out my phone like I was about to dial the territory healer registry.

"Then I'll contact every healer in this territory until I find out where she really is."

"You - ! Do you have to be this cold-blooded? Don't you care about your own pack at all?"

"Father, I'm twenty-five moons past my coming-of-age. Not five. I've seen your playbook a thousand times. I'm done playing along."

"You're always howling about honoring your elders, right? But your version of 'honor' is treating me like a tribute beast so you can pave a golden path for your son. Do you even deserve to call yourself a sire?"

He froze. His mouth opened and closed.

I took a breath and kept going.

"I earn thirty-two hundred credits a month. I send you twenty-four hundred. The rest goes to my den rent, food, and transport. It's been three cycles, and I haven't bought one new set of leathers. My pelt care routine? Whatever herbs I can scavenge."

"Meanwhile, you buy Lance custom combat gear and take him out for elk feasts. My fang was so infected my whole muzzle swelled, and I begged to keep an extra three hundred credits to get it treated. Mother gave me fifty. She acted like the rest was charity."

"Am I even your pup? I know you favor your son, but THIS IS INSANE!"

Father's face cycled through shades of red and white. His lips trembled. Nothing came out.

The crowd around us had grown thicker. Wolves murmured. Humans whispered.

"Are you kidding me? They're literally bleeding her dry to spoil their son. That's twisted."

"Right? And the sire has zero shame. I bet the dam's even worse."

"It's the modern era and wolves still pull this sexist prey-dung? That poor female."

Father's face bu//rned scarlet. He shot to his feet, jabbing his claw at me.

"I raised you! You think you don't owe me? Without me, you wouldn't even exist! You ungrateful little - "

"Father, did you forget? I paid for my Alpha-track education with blood loans. I covered my den costs by working three postings. The only thing you gave me was seed. What else have you ever done for me?"

He went completely still. Even his scent flatlined.

I grabbed my pack and turned to leave.

"Allie! Don't you dare - "

He roared behind me, a half-shift growl that made nearby travelers flinch.

I didn't stop.

Right as I was about to step through the gate barrier, he lunged forward and locked his arms around me from behind.

"Allie! You're not going anywhere!"

His grip was strong. Beta-enforcer strong. I couldn't break free.

My pack toppled over. Everything spilled - my spare leathers, my books, my moon-cycle charms. And the carved wooden sign I'd bought for my new den.

It said: [Keep running - you're just getting started.]

He stomped on it.

That's when my wolf snapped.

I whipped around and drove my elbow into his gut with everything I had.

He grunted. His grip broke. He staggered back, clutching his stomach, eyes wide with shock.

I didn't hesitate. I scooped up my scattered belongings, clawed them back into my pack, and sprinted through the gate barrier.

Behind me, I could hear Father cursing and gate sentries shouting him down.

It wasn't until I was on the moon-runner, strapped in, that I finally felt like I could breathe again.

As the runner lifted off, I watched the territory shrink below me. Trees and dens fading into patchwork green and brown. Tears streamed down my face. I let them.

Goodbye to my bloodsucking pack.

Goodbye to the life I'd been suffocating in.

The run was four hours.

When we touched down in the Houston territory, warm, thick air wrapped around me - nothing like the dry mountain cold back home.

I took a breath. Even my lungs felt lighter.

The Southern Range Pack sent Eileen to retrieve me. She was one of those she-wolves who smiled with her whole face, her energy warm and easy.

"Allie! Welcome! The Alpha told me to make sure you're completely settled."

She hauled my pack into the transport and handed me a cool drink.

"We're heading to your den first. Pack housing. You can rest - territory-hopping drains everyone."

The den sat in a clean, modern part of the city center. Two sleeping rooms. One bath. Sunlight poured through wide windows. Herbs grew in boxes on the balcony.

"This is part of your welcome offer. Free for three moons. After that, if you want to stay, you can lease it from the pack at a deep discount."

I stood in the bright common room, barely believing it.

This was a hundred times better than the glorified storage closet I'd been curled up in before.

"Thank you."

Eileen grinned, flashing a bit of fang. "No need! We're pack now. Get some rest. I'll retrieve you tomorrow for your blood oath and onboarding."

After she left, I wandered the den like I was dreaming.

I opened the cooling box. Fully stocked. Fresh meat. Cold drinks.

On the stone counter sat a basket of moonfruit with a card.

[Welcome to the Southern Range. Wishing you strong runs and good hunting.  - Phillip.]

I held the card. Traced the handwriting with my fingertip.

Something warm bloomed in my ch//est. Something I hadn't felt in years.

I changed into clean clothes and went down to the trading post below the den. Bought instant noodles.

Not because I couldn't afford better. Just out of habit.

But this time, I added a strip of sm0ked venison.

Sitting at the wide wooden table, eating steaming noodles, I realized this meal felt better than any feast my mother ever la!d out for Lance.

After I finished, I dealt with my bvsted travel pack. The leather strap was torn. One buckle had snapped clean off.

I pulled everything out and reorganized.

The carved wooden sign Father had stepped on - I cleaned it carefully with a damp cloth and hung it on the wall above my sleeping platform.

[Keep running - you're just getting started.]

The next day, I officially joined the pack.

The Southern Range was a growing pack-business. Good energy. Friendly wolves.

My posting was Project Lead. The tribute was several times what I'd been scraping by on before. I even had my own den-office.

The Alpha, Phillip Hastings, was young - maybe early thirties - but he carried himself with this quiet weight that made wolves listen.

He summoned me to his office for a quick word.

"Allie, I've reviewed your hunting record. The recruiter said you've got real potential and an iron discipline. I'm hoping you'll run far here."

"Thank you, Alpha Hastings. I'll give my best."

"Just Phillip." He smiled. "If you run into any issues, my den is always open."

I nodded and slipped out before my wolf could do anything embarrassing.

Work fell into rhythm fast. Houston territory moved at a quick clip, but I loved it.

I started tending to myself. Buying good leathers. New satchels.

On weekends, Eileen and I would hit up den-cafes, watch moon-runner races, try out all the best prey-houses in the city.

I also went to a real healer and got a full fang-and-claw checkup.

The healer said I had another wisdom fang that needed to come out.

I didn't hesitate. With numbing herbs, the whole thing was painless.

Lying in the chair, I thought about that nightmare extraction in the back-alley den. The silver pliers. The blood.

It felt like a lifetime ago.

One moon cycle later, I got my first full tribute payment.

I stared at the number in my pack account.

I finally understood what security felt like.

I moved out of the welcome den and leased an even nicer lair closer to the pack headquarters. I also signed up for moon-yoga sessions.

Little by little, my pelt got brighter. My wolf got calmer.

I thought I'd finally left the past in the dirt.

Then my phone buzzed. Unknown caller.

"This is Freya. Lance's intended mate."

I paused. Let the silence stretch.

"What do you want?"

Lottery day, my boyfriend blew up my phone. 
"Babe, I won! TWENTY MILLION DOLLARS!"
I was about to say congrats when he cut me off first.
"Wait wait wait—I'll send you your cut RIGHT NOW!"
So sweet.
My phone buzzed.
Venmo: $2.00 received.
Note: Ticket money. We're done.
I stared at those two bucks. 
Three years together, and that's ALL I was worth to him.
I smiled. Bitter. 
"Got it."
My hands shook as I hung up. Poured myself a drink.
What he didn't know? 
My ticket hit sixty million.

Lottery day, Jaxon's calls came in nonstop.

I picked up like fifteen times. My phone was bvrning hot in my hand.

"I WON! Chloe! I really won! Twenty million!"

His voice cracked on the other end, wild with this manic kind of joy.

He jumped in before I could speak. 

"Don't worry, I'm giving you your share right now!"

Something in my che//st warmed up a little at that.

Maybe he wasn't as bad as I thought.

My phone buzzed.

I opened Venmo.

New payment notification.

Amount: $2.00.

Note: Ticket money. We're square.

The air went dead quiet.

On the other end, Jaxon was still going off about his plans.

"I'm gonna get a car first, like a Porsche!" 

"Then I'll redo my mom's house—no wait, tear it down and build a whole new place! Three stories!" 

"And my mom needs surgery, so I'll get her top doctors!"

His voice sounded distant. 

All I could see was that two dollars.

We'd been together three years. Buying lottery tickets was our thing.

He'd pick the numbers. I'd pay. One ticket each.

Two bucks a ticket.

Today, he won twenty million.

And sent me two bucks back.

Square.

I almost laughed.

There was this fire stuck in my throat. It hurt to breathe.

"Got it."

"Great!" Jaxon sounded relieved. 

"Look, Chloe, you know things are different now."

"The gap between us... it's too big. It's not fair to you."

"You're a great girl. You'll find someone better for you."

He was actually giving me the "it's not you, it's me" speech.

"Yeah." I replied.

"I'll swing by later to grab some stuff. We can talk it through in person."

"Sure. Come over."

I hung up.

Went straight to the back of my drawer and pulled out MY ticket.

The numbers were based on my birthday.

I opened my phone. Pulled up the winning numbers. Checked them one by one.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

Every single number matched.

First prize. Power Play.

Sixty million dollars.

I carefully put the ticket back in the drawer and locked it.

Then I walked into the living room and flipped our photo frame facedown on the table.

I did the math.

From his place to mine, forty minutes if traffic was good.

Right now, he'd be heading to the bank to confirm. 

Calling his family. 

Probably blowing up the group chat with cash drops.

By the time he remembered me—his "ex"—it'd be at least two hours.

Plenty of time.

I opened my laptop and searched "best divorce lawyer in Portland."

We weren't married.

But they'd have the most experience with messy financial stuff.

I picked the most expensive one and called the assistant.

"Hi, I need legal advice on property transfers and asset agreements."

"I need a contract with full legal standing."

"Rush job. I'll pay triple."

The assistant's voice was all business.

"Can you give me an estimate of the asset value?"

"We need to assess the scope and risk."

I looked out the window. Sky was gray. Looked like rain.

"A property. And... some verbal promises that might come up later."

I paused.

"Also, I need a lawyer at my place in two hours. With recording equipment."

"Of course, ma'am. Can you provide your address?"

I gave it to her and hung up.

Only then did I realize how thirsty I was.

I poured myself ice water and downed it in one go.

Slammed the glass on the table. It made a loud thud.

Jaxon, you better not let me down.

Do your worst.

The doorbell rang exactly two hours later.

Even faster than I expected.

I looked through the peephole.

Two people standing there.

Jaxon. And his mom.

The smug look on Linda's face was practically oozing through the door.

I took a deep breath and unlocked it.

The door swung open, and I got hit with this thick cloud of cheap perfume.

Mixed with that gross new-money energy.

Jaxon stood behind his mom, avoiding my eyes.

Linda, though? 

She walked in like she owned the place. 

"Chloe. Place hasn't changed much, huh."

Like she was commenting on a dump she never liked anyway.

I didn't say anything. Just stepped aside to let them in.

Jaxon kicked off his shoes and stood there awkwardly in the entryway.

Linda, however, walked right in wearing those brand-new heels with the fake diamonds glued on.

Click. Click. Click.

"Jaxon's different now." 

Linda finally looked back at me. Straight to the point. 

"He won twenty million. That's life-changing."

"Our whole family hit the jackpot."

I looked at her. Nodded. 

"Congrats."

My calm seemed to piss her off. 

"You're a smart girl."

"You get how important it is to be with someone on your level." 

Her tone dripped with fake pity. 

"Before, I thought you were fine for Jaxon." 

"But now? You make what, ten grand a month?"

"Compared to my son, you're dirt."

Jaxon's face went red, then white. 

He tugged on her sleeve.

"Mom, stop."

Linda yanked her arm away. Her voice shot up. 

"Which part isn't true? You're too soft, son!" 

"I'm not letting some girl take advantage of you!"

"This apartment—when we bought it, we put down two hundred thousand."

"Her family didn't pay a dime!"

"You insisted on putting her name on it for 'security' or whatever."

"Well, now you're breaking up. What happens to the apartment?"

There it was.

That's why they came.

I wanted to laugh, but I kept my face blank.

"Linda, you're remembering it wrong." 

My voice was quiet but clear. 

"The down payment was five hundred thousand total." 

"My family paid three hundred. Yours paid two hundred."

"Jaxon said that two hundred was part of the engagement money." 

"An advance." 

"I've been paying the mortgage ever since. Eight thousand a month." 

"I've got bank records and receipts for all of it."

Linda's face turned purple.

She didn't expect me to remember. Or fight back.

"You... you're lying!"

"We gave two hundred thousand, that's a fact!" 

"Engagement money only counts if you actually get married." 

"Since you're not, that's a loan!"

She was just making stuff up now.

"Mom!" Jaxon finally snapped at her.

He turned to me. His eyes were begging. Guilty.

"Chloe, let's just talk this out."

"The apartment... look, I won the lottery. I'm obviously gonna buy a mansion now." 

"But this place—my mom's money went into it. They want it back."

"For... for my brother. When he gets married."

I stared at him.

A few hours ago, he was telling me he loved me. 

That he'd give me a home.

Now he was dragging his college-aged brother into this just to take back the apartment.

"So you want me to give you the apartment back?" I asked.

"Not give back—return what's ours!" 

Linda jumped in. 

"It should've been ours all along!"

"Fine."

The second those words left my mouth, the whole room went silent.

Jaxon and Linda both froze. 

They probably had this whole plan ready—threats, guilt trips, tantrums. 

They didn't expect me to just agree.

Jaxon's eyes lit up for a second. Then guilt crept back in.

Linda didn't even try to hide her greed.

"You serious?" she asked, testing me.

"Yeah." I nodded. 

"But I have one condition."

"I knew it!" Linda's guard shot back up. 

"How much do you want?" 

"Listen, Chloe, don't get greedy." 

"That twenty million is Jaxon's. You don't get a cent of it!" 

"That two bucks he sent you? That was generous!"

"I don't want money." 

I looked right at them. 

"I just want everything in writing. An agreement."

"What kind of agreement?" Jaxon asked.

"A property settlement and relationship termination agreement." 

I'd rehearsed this part. 

"I'll transfer the apartment to you for free." 

"But we need to make a few things crystal clear in writing."

I paused and looked between the two of them.

"First. You, Jaxon, initiated the breakup." 

"The reason?" 

"You won twenty million and decided the financial gap between us was too big. We're not compatible anymore."

Jaxon's expression shifted slightly.

"Second. The two hundred thousand your family put toward the down payment wasn't a loan." 

"It was an engagement gift." 

"I'm voluntarily giving up my claim to it and returning the entire property."

"Third. And this is the important one." 

I looked at Linda. Let a tiny smile touch my lips. 

"The agreement states that once you take back the apartment, we're done."

"All financial ties, all emotional ties—wiped clean."

"You go your way, I go mine."

"You can't come after me for anything ever again."

My terms sounded perfect for them.

I was giving back the apartment, taking all the blame, and promising to disappear forever.

Jaxon's whole body relaxed. 

He let out this huge breath like he'd just dodged a bullet.

Linda only had eyes for the apartment. 

"Where's the contract? Let's sign it now!"

"Hold on." I checked my phone. 

"I already called a lawyer." 

"They're bringing a proper contract and recording equipment." 

"Everything we sign will be legally binding."

"A lawyer? What a waste of money!" 

Linda muttered, but she looked even happier.

To her, hiring a lawyer just meant I was making this "unequal treaty" more official. More secure for her.

Jaxon chimed in. 

"Chloe, isn't this a bit much..."

"It's necessary." 

I cut him off. My tone left no room for argument. 

"This protects both of us." 

"Let's get it done right. No loose ends."

The doorbell rang.

I went to answer it.

A middle-aged man in a sharp suit stood there with his young assistant.

He nodded at me. 

"Ms. Bennett. I'm Mr. Harrison."

I let them in and gestured toward Jaxon and Linda. 

"Mr. Harrison, these are the other parties."

Mr. Harrison's eyes swept over them with that cool, professional lawyer stare. 

Even Linda seemed to shrink a little under it.

I clapped my hands lightly. 

"Let's get started."

The assistant moved quickly, setting up a small camera and voice recorder on the coffee table.

The little red lights blinked in the dim living room.

Like tiny eyes watching every greedy intention.

Mr. Harrison worked fast.

He pulled a pre-drafted agreement out of his briefcase. 

The title read: 

"Voluntary Agreement Regarding Termination of Relationship and Property Settlement."

"Ms. Bennett, Mr. Reed, Ms. Reed." 

His voice was calm and professional. 

"Per Ms. Bennett's request, I've prepared this agreement." 

"I'll now go through it line by line."

"To ensure all parties' true intentions are captured, per my client's instructions, this entire process is being recorded."

Linda and Jaxon glanced at each other. 

This whole setup felt a bit much.

But the thought of walking away with a half-million-dollar apartment without a fight? 

They could sit through it.

"Article One: Party A (Ms. Chloe Bennett) and Party B (Mr. Jaxon Reed) voluntarily agree to officially terminate their romantic relationship as of today."

Mr. Harrison looked up at Jaxon. 

"Mr. Reed, did you initiate this breakup?"

Jaxon's jaw twitched. 

He looked at his mom, then at me. 

Finally, he nodded. "Yeah."

"And the reason?" 

Mr. Harrison pressed, like a robot with no feelings.

"I... I won the lottery. Twenty million." 

"I just... we don't work anymore." 

Jaxon's voice was barely a whisper.

"Noted." Mr. Harrison scribbled in his notepad. 

"Article Two: This property is currently registered under Ms. Chloe Bennett."

"After mutual discussion, she voluntarily agrees to transfer 100% ownership to Mr. Jaxon Reed, free of charge."

Linda's breathing sped up.

"Mr. Harrison, can we add a detail here?" I spoke up suddenly.

Everyone's eyes snapped to me.

Linda's expression turned suspicious. 

"What are you trying to add?"

"Relax, Linda." I smiled gently. 

"Just making sure the facts are clear."

"Mr. Harrison, please note that the down payment for this property was five hundred thousand dollars total." 

"Party A, Ms. Chloe Bennett, contributed three hundred thousand."

"Party B's mother, Ms. Linda Reed, contributed two hundred thousand."

"You—" Linda started to snap.

I kept going. 

"Also note that Ms. Linda Reed's two hundred thousand was given as an engagement gift." 

"It was not a loan."

"Now, since the marriage will not take place, Party A, Ms. Chloe Bennett, voluntarily returns the entire property to Party B."

My words sounded like legal jargon.

But the logic was airtight.

I completely shut down any claim that it was a "loan." 

I defined it as a "conditional gift." 

And now, I was "voluntarily" giving it up.

Jaxon and Linda didn't know much about the law. 

To them, it sounded perfect.

"Fine! Write it exactly like that!" 

Linda waved her hand, scared I'd change my mind.

Mr. Harrison nodded and quickly added the amendment to the agreement.

"Article Three: Upon signing this agreement, Party A, Party B will have no further financial or emotional entanglements." 

"Party B may not interfere with Party A's life for any reason." 

"In the event of violation, the breaching party will pay the non-breaching party damages for emotional distress in the amount of..."

Mr. Harrison paused and looked at me. 

"Ms. Bennett, what amount would you like to specify?"

I looked at Jaxon's face. Took my time.

"Twenty million."

"WHAT?" 

Jaxon and Linda both shot out of their seats.

"Are you insane? What gives you the right?" Linda shrieked.

"Linda, relax." 

I kept my voice calm. 

"It's just a deterrent clause." 

"The whole point of this agreement is that I'm giving you the apartment." 

"I only have one request—that you leave me alone afterward." 

"As long as you can do that, this clause never comes into play." 

"You're getting a half-million-dollar apartment in exchange for a promise to never bother me again." 

"That's fair, isn't it?"

My words had this weird persuasive quality.

To them, they were getting everything. 

Why would they ever need to come after me? 

They'd be the ones avoiding me.

This clause was just a pathetic security blanket for the loser. That's how they saw it.

Jaxon hesitated.

But Linda had already made up her mind for him.

"Fine! Twenty million, whatever!"

"Who cares about bothering you? Sign it!"

Mr. Harrison printed three copies of the finalized agreement and laid them on the coffee table.

"If everything looks correct, please sign."

Linda snatched up a pen and practically stabbed her signature onto the paper.

Jaxon signed right after.

I picked up my pen and carefully wrote "Chloe Bennett" in the Party A section.

Once the agreement was signed, Mr. Harrison and his assistant packed up and politely excused themselves.

I walked them to the door. 

Mr. Harrison spoke quietly. 

"Ms. Bennett, all audio and video files have been backed up."

"The agreement is now in effect."

"I'll make sure they move quickly on the property transfer."

"Thanks, Mr. Harrison."

I closed the door. 

Only the three of us left in the living room now.

Linda held that agreement. 

The wrinkles on her face stretched with her grin.

"Alright, Chloe, we won't stick around."

"We'll send people to clear out the apartment in a couple days."

"You pack up your personal stuff and get out soon." Her tone was all orders.

"Sure."

"Jaxon, let's go! We need to tell your dad the good news!"

Linda grabbed Jaxon and marched toward the door like a general who'd just won a war.

Jaxon paused while putting his shoes back on. 

He glanced back at me.

His expression was complicated. 

Relief. Guilt. And something else I couldn't quite read. 

Pity, maybe.

He probably thought I'd lost everything.

Some pathetic girl who got dumped for millions, and stupidly gave away her only asset.

"Chloe," he finally said. 

"I'm sorry. You... take care of yourself."

I looked at him. Didn't say a word.

The door slammed shut.

Complete silence.

I walked to the window. Watched them get into a brand-new white BMW parked downstairs. 

Probably Jaxon's first car. 

Not the Porsche he'd dreamed of, but close enough.

The engine started. They disappeared into traffic.

I pulled out my phone and dialed another number.

"Hi, is this the Oregon Lottery office?" 

"I'd like to ask—do I need to make an appointment to claim a sixty-million-dollar prize?"

On the other end, the lottery office rep sounded formal.

"Ma'am, for prizes over ten million, we recommend scheduling an appointment at least one day in advance."

"Weekday mornings work best."

"We'll set up a private process to protect your privacy and security."

"Okay. I'd like to book tomorrow at nine a.m."

"May I have your name?"

"Bennett. Chloe Bennett."

"Perfect, Ms. Bennett. See you tomorrow."

I hung up.

Stood there in the empty living room.

Felt like I'd just woken up from the longest, most ridiculous dream.

The ceiling light was harsh and white. 

Made the black ink on that agreement look even sharper.

I walked over, picked up my copy, and took a clear photo with my phone. 

Uploaded it to an encrypted cloud drive.

Then I locked it in the back of a drawer. Right next to my lottery ticket.

I didn't have much to pack.

Three years. I thought I was building a home. 

Every single thing I bought was about the future.

Turns out I was just decorating a temporary space for some bas//tard.

I opened the closet. Only took my own clothes.

Anything he bought me? Left it all behind. 

All those couple things we bought together. 

Movie ticket stubs. Souvenirs from trips. 

I didn't even look at them.

I only took one small picture frame. Me and my parents.

An hour later, I was standing at the door with a carry-on suitcase.

I looked back one last time at this apartment—

I'd paid most of the down payment for. 

The mortgage I'd covered for three years.

Then I shut the door behind me. Didn't look back.

The elevator went down. 

Numbers counting backward. 

Like a countdown to leaving my past behind.

I walked out of the building. Didn't call a ride. Just walked.

The evening breeze hit my face. Cool. 

I needed somewhere to stay.

I pulled out my phone. Went straight for the best five-star in the city.

Booked an executive suite. Paid upfront for a week.

When I walked into that lobby—marble floors, thick carpets, chandeliers—the front desk didn't even blink.

Here, money was the only ID that mattered.

I got to my suite. 

First thing I did? 

Pulled all my clothes out of the suitcase and called housekeeping for laundry service.

Then I walked into the huge bathroom and turned on the shower. 

Let the hot water run over me.

Steam filled the whole space. 

My reflection in the mirror went blurry.

I don't know how long I stood there. 

Long enough for my skin to turn red from the heat.

I wrapped myself in a robe and walked to the floor-to-ceiling window.

Thirty floors up. 

The city below looked like rivers of light flowing through the streets.

And me? I felt like a ghost floating in midair.

My phone rang.

Unknown number.

I picked up.

"Ms. Bennett, hi. This is Emily, Mr. Harrison's assistant." 

"About the financial advisor you requested—"

"We've set up a meeting with Mr. Carter. He's the best in the business." 

"He's available tomorrow at two p.m. Does that work for you?"

"Yeah. That works." My voice sounded rough.

"Great. Also, Mr. Harrison wanted me to remind you—"

"The other party is pushing hard to finalize the property transfer."

"They're planning to go first thing tomorrow morning." 

"You'll need to be there to sign."

"Got it."

"Ms. Bennett... are you okay?" The assistant hesitated. 

Like she could hear the exhaustion in my voice.

I tried to smile, even though she couldn't see me.

"I'm fine."

I hung up and collapsed onto the soft bed.

Sixty million dollars.

The number kept circling in my head.

But it didn't make me happy at all.

It just showed how ug1y and greedy people could be.

But it was also a shield. 

Something to keep me breathing when the whole world turned its back on me.

I didn't sleep all night.

Next morning at nine, I showed up at the lottery office right on time.

No crowds. No chaos. 

They led me through a private entrance into a quiet office.

The director handled everything personally. 

Verified the ticket. Checked my ID. Processed the claim.

The whole thing went insanely fast.

After taxes—twenty percent—and a donation I chose to make? 

This astronomical number landed in my new bank account.

I walked out holding that thin piece of plastic. 

The sunlight was blinding.

Next stop: the property records office.

Jaxon and Linda were already waiting.

The second Linda saw me, her face dropped. 

Jaxon was head-to-toe designer brands. New gold watch on his wrist.

When he saw me, this flash of superiority crossed his face. 

Then he switched to fake impatience.

"What took you so long? We've been waiting forever!" Linda snapped.

I ignored her. Walked straight to the counter.

Signed the papers. Pressed my thumbprint.

When the clerk handed Jaxon the new deed, Linda snatched it out of his hands and clutched it to her che//st. 

Pure joy all over her face.

"Son! The apartment's ours! It's finally ours!"

Jaxon let out this huge breath. 

Looked at me like he'd just finished some annoying chore.

"Chloe, we're even now. For good."

"Yep." I nodded.

I turned and walked out.

Behind me, Linda's voice got louder on purpose.

"Oh, honey, we gotta celebrate tonight!"

"Invite all the relatives over to our new place!"

"Let everyone see how successful we are now!"

I kept walking. Didn't stop. Left the building.

At two p.m., I met with Mr. Carter, the financial advisor.

Mid-forties. Polished. Calm.

We talked for three hours.

I split my money into different buckets. 

Real estate investments. Conservative funds. Emergency cash. 

And I set up an anonymous trust.

By the time we finished, it was dark outside.

I got back to the hotel. One unread message on my phone.

From a mutual friend.

A screenshot. From Jaxon's Instagram.

The photo showed my old apartment packed with people. Total mess.

Jaxon and Linda stood in the center. 

Linda holding up that property deed like a trophy.

Jaxon's caption:

"New life starts now! Grateful for the past, but it's just a chapter."

"At the end of the day, you gotta rely on yourself!"

Tons of likes and comments kissing up to him.

I stared at that line—"you gotta rely on yourself"—and actually laughed.

Right then, another call came in. 

Unknown number.

I answered.

Linda's sharp voice. 

"Chloe, we found another lottery ticket on your desk."

"What's that about?!"

"Her family is poor, from a low-ranking rogue lineage by the way. No matter how good she is, a girl like that is only meant to be played with."
 
I felt my blood boil and my stomach churn. I trembled slightly, my nails digging deep into my palms as I took sharp breaths to suppress my rising fury. But when I heard that familiar voice, I couldn't hold back anymore.
 
"It's hard to say," Xavier said. "I'm not in a rush to choose a fated mate. I can play around for another two years."

~~~
 
Everything went to shit after that but when I left there, I didn't go home immediately. Instead, I went into a nearby rogue-friendly bar. It wasn't that I was intentionally trying to get blackout drunk. I just had nothing else to do, so I ordered a pitcher of liquor and sipped it slowly, watching the lively crowd on the dance floor like an outsider. My mind was in an absolute frenzy, but before I could make a final decision, the elevator dinged loudly as we reached our destination.
 
Killian stepped out into the grand, dimly lit penthouse foyer first, leaving behind a completely nonchalant explanation. "I gave you the password so you can come and go easily over the next few days. You should be able to find a permanent place and move this weekend."
 
Does this man have actual mind-reading abilities? I thought, gritting my teeth. Unfortunately, I was completely cornered by my own safety concerns, so I could only swallow my anxiety, endure the mental torment, and follow him inside.
 
However, a wave of immense relief washed over me the moment I stepped through the main doors. The interior space was absolutely massive, sprawling across the entire top floor.
 
With a place this big, I was absolutely certain I would have my own private room to sleep in without being anywhere near him.
 
Feeling a bit more relaxed, I bent down at the entryway to re-tie the leather straps of my high heels, which had come loose during the walk.
 
As I did, I heard his deep voice echo from just a few feet ahead of me. "There are several empty guest rooms down the hall. You can choose whichever one you like."
 
I stood up straight, but before I could even open my mouth to say thank you, a small white object shot out from my chest with a sharp ‘ping’, flying through the air and hitting Killian squarely in the middle of his back.
 
The two of us instantly froze, facing each other in the quiet hallway.
 
I glanced down out of the corner of my eye, and my breath caught instantly in my throat.
 
It had ripped.
 
The straining button on the front of the replacement shirt he had bought me had finally snapped under the pressure of my chest, completely popping off and leaving the front of the shirt gaping open. I stood there, utterly paralyzed with mortification.
 
Killian turned around slowly, his dark eyes sweeping down over my exposed collarbone and the gap in the fabric before he looked away, his voice entirely light and even. "This shirt is clearly a bit too small for you."
 
I blushed instantly, a fierce heat rushing up my neck until my face was bright red to the roots of my hair. I felt like I had been repeatedly dunked in boiling water.
 
Without a word, I silently scrambled to scoop the broken button off the hardwood floor, held my handbag horizontally across my chest like a shield, and casually plunged into the very first bedroom door I could reach to escape his gaze.
 
"That room is..."
 
I heard his voice start to caution me from the hallway, but I didn't care. I was fleeing in absolute disarray. I slammed the door behind me, only to immediately realize what was wrong. The room smelled overwhelmingly of dark cedar, leather, and pure Alpha dominance. It was distinctly his.
 
My face felt like it was about to bleed from sheer embarrassment and the overwhelming scent of him. Turning on my heel, I bolted right back out into the hallway, completely losing my composure.
 
I was moving so fast and was so thoroughly mortified that I didn't even notice Killian was still standing right outside the frame. I ran headfirst straight into his broad chest.
 
"Ah..." I gasped as the impact rattled my face. My nose throbbed painfully, and the sudden sting instantly triggered my tear ducts, causing my eyes to well up with involuntary tears.
 
I subconsciously looked up at him through a blurry, watery gaze, my eyes sparkling with a mix of pain and intense shyness.
 
My naturally fair skin was completely flushed like ripe cherries, making me look utterly defenseless, delicate, and entirely exposed.
 
As I stood trapped against him, the natural, sweet fragrance of my skin flared from the stress, completely enveloping him in the narrow hallway.
 
I felt Killian's breathing stutter, turning slightly heavier as he felt my soft shape pressed directly into his arms. His dark gaze gradually deepened, a dangerous, primal spark flickering in the depths of his eyes.
 
"This is my room," he murmured, his voice dropping into a low, raspy register.
 
Hearing him speak like that made my heart pound frantically against my ribs. He sounded less like a cold, distant corporate CEO and more like something inexplicably alluring.
 
My pulse raced. I bit my lip hard, letting out a faint, embarrassed "Oh," before I twisted out of his grip, turned around, and quickly slipped into the guest bedroom next door, shutting the door firmly behind me.
 
~~~
 
Once safely inside the proper guest room, I rushed through washing my face and quickly climbed into the large bed, desperate to put the chaotic evening behind me.
 
However, the moment I pulled the heavy comforter up to my chin knock echoed against the wood of my door.
 
My muscles tensed up involuntarily. I gripped the edge of the blanket tightly, hesitating in the dark for a long moment before raising my voice to call out, "What's wrong?"
 
"I brought some ointment for your wrists. You might need it," Killian’s voice drifted through the door.
 
I sat up slowly, shifting the covers aside.
 
The words he spoke were cool, aloof, and completely devoid of any underlying desire or hidden meaning.
 
His tone left absolutely no room for a wandering imagination, making the intense tension of the previous night feel like nothing more than a fever dream.
 
I shook my head vigorously to clear the lingering fog from my brain and looked down at my hands.
 
Xavier had gripped my skin with so much force during the struggle in the archives room that my skin was covered in ugly, dark bruises and shallow scratches where his nails had dug in.
 
"Just a second, I'm coming," I called out.
 
I quickly smoothed down my clothes, slipped my feet into my shoes, and walked over to swing the door open.
 
Killian was standing there holding a small tube of medical ointment. He handed it over without a word, gave me a brief nod, and turned right back around to walk to his own room.
 
I stood in the doorway, staring down at the unopened tube in my hand, feeling a sudden warmth in my chest.
 
No matter how cold or intimidating he chose to be, Killian had gone out of his way to protect and look after me today.
 
~~~
 
Despite the safety of the penthouse, I didn't sleep well at all. The trauma from Xavier’s attack followed me into the dark, plaguing me with restless, exhausting nightmares all through the night.
 
When my alarm finally went off in the morning, my head felt heavy and my brain was completely groggy.
 
Still, I forced myself out of bed and navigated my way into the kitchen. Part of it was because my stomach was completely empty, but the larger part was because I wanted to find a way to properly thank Killian for taking me in when I had nowhere else to go.
 
I found a wealth of fresh groceries stocked in the massive stainless-steel refrigerator. I pulled out ingredients and quickly set to work, losing myself in the rhythm of cooking.
 
A short while later, the sound of footsteps signaled Killian entering the space.
 
I didn't see him look at me, but I adjusted the apron around my waist, my hair loosely tied up with a few stray strands falling gently around my face as the morning sunlight streamed through the floor-to-ceiling windows behind me.
 
I plated the food and turned around to carry the dishes to the long dining table, only to find him standing much closer than I expected, watching me silently.
 
The sudden sight of him startled me so much that I nearly dropped the plates, freezing in my tracks.
 
Seeing him staring at me with that unreadable expression, I felt a familiar shyness creep up my neck. I quickly cleared my throat to explain myself. "I noticed you had a lot of fresh groceries in the fridge. I know someone like you definitely won't accept rent money from me, but I really don't feel comfortable staying here completely for free. I'm actually a pretty decent cook, so please consider breakfast as my payment for the room, okay?"
 
In truth, when I had first opened the refrigerator and seen it piled high with fresh fruits, vegetables, and high-quality ingredients, I simply couldn't resist.
 
I honestly hadn't expected a powerful, solitary Alpha who seemed entirely unaccustomed to domestic life to keep such a warm, homey, and fully stocked kitchen.
 
Killian didn't show much expression on his handsome face. He merely gave a slight nod and said, "Thank you for your hard work," in a light, even tone before consciously moving over to take a seat at the table.
 
I set down the meal I had prepared: a golden scallion and ham egg roll, a plate of crispy shrimp potstickers, and a steaming bowl of traditional savory congee with preserved egg and lean pork. It was a simple, comforting, yet deeply satisfying breakfast.
 
He ate efficiently and in total silence. Once he finished his portion, Killian set his chopsticks down on the rest, pulled a linen napkin to slowly wipe his mouth, and said emotionlessly, "It tasted very good."
 
His delivery was completely flat, merely stating an objective fact, exactly the same way he had handed over the five million dollar check after our first night together.
 
Over the past two days, I had managed to get a general idea of what kind of temperament my new boss possessed. If I had to describe him to anyone, I would say he was completely emotionless and frighteningly calm at all times.
 
That kind of detached personality made him an absolute terror in the legal world, his cold-blooded nature allowed him to rationally analyze and dismantle every single variable in a case without ever letting personal feelings get in the way.
 
He truly deserved his reputation as the undefeated warrior of the high court.
 
Since there was absolutely no personal emotion tied to his compliment, I didn't let it fluster me. I simply listened to the praise and offered a polite, professional smile. "I'm glad you liked it."
 
Killian stood up from the table, his sharp eyes dropping for a fraction of a second to the front of my chest.
 
Because the button had popped last night, I had been forced to use a thin piece of spare twine to hastily tie the fabric together, and the makeshift fix was barely holding the shirt closed against my skin.
 
He buttoned his suit jacket and checked his watch. "I've already had a selection of professional attire delivered and placed in the living room for you. As a practicing lawyer, I shouldn't need to elaborate on the importance of proper courtroom attire."
 
He paused at the edge of the kitchen, turning back slightly. "There's no need for you to clear the table or wash the dishes. A housekeeper will be here shortly to handle the cleaning."
 
I felt a sudden flush of embarrassment heat my cheeks. My formal suits for actual court appearances were incredibly high quality and immaculate. It was only my regular, everyday office wear that was a bit more ordinary.
 
"I..." I started, wanting to say thank you, but the word caught in my throat.
 
Watching his tall silhouette vanish out the front door, I slowly swallowed the rest of my sentence.
 
Even though he had mentioned a housekeeper was on the way, I still gathered the plates and carried them over to the sink to wash them out of sheer politeness.
 
After all, regardless of our strange history, this was still his home, and I refused to be a burden.
